title: Expand the Set of Options to Produce Higher-Quality Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that the surest way to improve decision quality is to generate more options before choosing. It cites three decades of research and compares narrow option sets to shopping from a single clothes rack. The post lists sources of alternatives: the team, other institutions and subject-matter experts. It insists on separating option generation from evaluation, so that choices are judged on outcomes, risks and benefits only after a full slate exists. The closing claim is that a larger set of options also helps leaders build conviction to decide.
points: Research over three decades links a larger set of viable options to a higher chance of finding a great decision.
Narrow option sets produce average choices, like buying clothes from only one rack.
Other institutions and subject-matter experts are named as concrete sources of new alternatives.
Generate first and evaluate second: options are judged on outcomes, risks and benefits only once the full range exists.
quotes: The best decision-makers don’t settle for a small set or slate of solutions, approaches, or strategies. They work hard to expand that list to give them the best chance of landing on a great choice.

Limiting the selection of decision options is akin to buying clothes only from one rack. Until we take the opportunity to learn about what else is out there, we make selections that are more average than they should be.
In addition to exploring the possible options with the team, leaders can also look to other institutions and learn what choices they have made to address a problem or opportunity.
Asking experts to engage in out-of-the-box thinking with the primary goal of identifying plausible alternatives will often produce a breakthrough and put several new options on the table.
Once a full range of possibilities exists, decision-makers can systematically evaluate them for probable outcomes, risks, and benefits.
By having more choices to consider, decision-makers often find a great option among them and can quickly build the conviction needed to decide.
